claims.text: The simulated alloy is equiatomic FeNiCrMn with an FCC crystal structure.
The initial FeNiCrMn structure contains pre-existing vacancy clusters and surface defects.
Dislocations nucleate primarily at vacancy clusters or surface defects.
Local stress concentrations at vacancy clusters or surfaces exceed the Peierls barrier and emit Shockley partial dislocations.
Loading along <11-1> produces a higher maximum yield stress than loading along <110>.
The proposed orientation dependence is governed by Schmid-factor differences for FCC {111}<110> slip.
The <11-1> orientation is generally harder for FCC slip than <110> under the relevant loading configuration.
The HCP-like regions in FeNiCrMn are intrinsic stacking faults rather than a true HCP or martensitic phase transformation.
Perfect FCC dislocations with Burgers vector a/2<110> dissociate into Shockley partials with Burgers vector a/6<112>, producing HCP-like stacking at an intrinsic stacking fault.
FeNiCrMn has low stacking-fault energy that favors partial-dislocation emission over perfect-dislocation glide.
Dislocation density increases with strain rate because high rates leave insufficient time for dislocation annihilation.
Yield strength is relatively insensitive to strain rate from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
Yield strength decreases monotonically as temperature increases.
CNA should identify stacking faults as local HCP coordination embedded within an FCC environment without long-range HCP periodicity.
An intrinsic stacking fault should exhibit a local ABCABC-to-ABAB stacking change without a distinct unit-cell volume or symmetry change.
Long-range HCP periodicity and a distinct HCP lattice-parameter or symmetry change would indicate a true phase transformation rather than an isolated stacking fault.
CoNiCrFeMn can undergo simultaneous twinning and martensitic transformation at 300 K under tensile MD loading.
The proposed mechanism is limited to FCC equiatomic FeNiCrMn and is not expected to apply to high-stacking-fault-energy alloys where perfect dislocations dominate.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes the higher <11-1> yield stress both to a maximized Schmid factor and to a higher applied stress required for slip. For a fixed critical resolved shear stress, maximizing the Schmid factor normally lowers the required applied stress, so the stated geometric explanation conflicts with the predicted harder orientation.

The hypothesis confidently states that <11-1> has higher yield stress, whereas the mechanism says this orientation may maximize resolved shear stress or require higher applied stress 'depending on' slip-plane activation. These alternatives do not establish a single consistent directional prediction.
